Iron reacts with steam as \(3Fe + 4H_{2}O \rightarrow Fe_{3}O_{4} + 4H_{2}\).

Moles of steam \(= 18/18 = 1\) mol.

From the balanced equation, 4 mol of \(H_{2}O\) consume 3 mol of Fe, so 1 mol of \(H_{2}O\) consumes \(3/4 = 0.75\) mol of Fe.

Mass of Fe \(= 0.75 \times 56 = 42\) g. Iron is in excess, so steam is limiting and the answer is 42 g.

\(Li^{2+}\) is a one-electron (hydrogen-like) species with \(Z = 3\), its single electron being in \(n = 1\).

For a hydrogen-like ion the ionization energy is \(IE = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\) J per atom.

So \(IE = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \frac{3^{2}}{1^{2}} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 9 = 1.962 \times 10^{-17}\) J per atom.

Bond orders from MO theory: \(O_{2}^{+}\) 2.5, \(O_{2}\) 2.0, \(O_{2}^{-}\) 1.5, \(O_{2}^{2-}\) 1.0. Bond length varies inversely with bond order, so the length order is \(O_{2}^{+} < O_{2} < O_{2}^{-} < O_{2}^{2-}\). Statement I is true.

Unpaired electrons in the \(\pi^{*}\) set: \(O_{2}\) has 2, \(O_{2}^{+}\) has 1, \(O_{2}^{-}\) has 1, \(O_{2}^{2-}\) has 0. Since \(O_{2}^{+}\) and \(O_{2}^{-}\) both carry exactly one unpaired electron, the strict inequality \(O_{2}^{+} > O_{2}^{-}\) is wrong. Statement II is false.

Hence Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

Moles of acid \(= 19.5/78 = 0.25\) mol in 0.5 kg water, so molality \(m = 0.5\) mol kg\(^{-1}\) (and molarity is taken as 0.5 M).

\(\Delta T_{f} = i K_{f} m \Rightarrow 1 = i \times 1.86 \times 0.5 \Rightarrow i = 1.0753\).

For a monobasic acid \(HA \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + A^{-}\), \(i = 1 + \alpha\), so \(\alpha = 0.0753\).

\(K_{a} = \frac{C\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha} = \frac{0.5 \times (0.0753)^{2}}{0.9247} = \frac{2.835 \times 10^{-3}}{0.9247} \approx 3.07 \times 10^{-3}\).

The half cell with the higher reduction potential acts as the cathode: \(AgBr/Ag,Br^{-}\) at \(+0.07\) V. The \(Fe(OH)_{2}/Fe\) couple at \(-0.88\) V is therefore reversed and acts as the anode.

Anode: \(Fe(s) + 2OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_{2}(s) + 2e^{-}\)
Cathode: \(2AgBr(s) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Ag(s) + 2Br^{-}(aq)\)
Overall: \(Fe(s) + 2OH^{-}(aq) + 2AgBr(s) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_{2}(s) + 2Ag(s) + 2Br^{-}(aq)\), which is option (A).

Checking the others: \(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = 0.07 - (-0.88) = +0.95\) V, not \(-0.95\) V, so (B) is wrong; Fe is oxidised, not reduced, so (C) is wrong; electrode potential is an intensive property, so (D) is wrong.

Zero order: \([A] = [A]_{0} - kt\). Completion means \([A] = 0\), so \(t_{100\%} = [A]_{0}/k\), while \(t_{1/2} = [A]_{0}/2k\). Hence \(t_{100\%} = 2t_{1/2}\).

First order: \(t = \frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}\). As \([A] \rightarrow 0\) the logarithm diverges, so a first order reaction never reaches 100 percent completion and \(t_{100\%}\) is infinite, written in the options as \((t_{1/2})^{\infty}\).

The pairing zero order then first order is therefore \(t_{100\%} = 2t_{1/2}\) and \(t_{100\%} = (t_{1/2})^{\infty}\).

Statement I: first ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol\(^{-1}\)) are Na 496, Mg 738, Cl 1251, Ar 1521, i.e. they increase left to right across period 3: \(Na < Mg < Cl < Ar\). The stated order \(Na > Mg > Cl > Ar\) is exactly reversed, so Statement I is false.

Statement II: removing a third electron from Ca means breaking into the stable \(Ca^{2+}\) noble gas core \([Ar]\), so \(IE_{3}(Ca) \approx 4912\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\), far larger than for Al (2745), Fe (2957) or B (3660). Statement II is true.

Hence Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

Standard reduction potentials fall down group 17, so oxidising power decreases as \(F_{2} > Cl_{2} > Br_{2} > I_{2}\). Statement I is true.

Because \(Cl_{2}\) is a stronger oxidant than \(Br_{2}\) or \(I_{2}\), chlorine water liberates free halogen from a bromide or iodide, \(Cl_{2} + 2Br^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + Br_{2}\) and \(Cl_{2} + 2I^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + I_{2}\). The liberated halogen is extracted into an organic layer, giving the characteristic orange-brown (\(Br_{2}\)) or violet (\(I_{2}\)) colour of the layer test. This is a displacement redox reaction, so Statement II is true and correctly explains the basis of the test.

1,2,3-Trihydroxypropane is glycerol. Glycerol decomposes at or near its normal boiling point, so it is purified by distillation under reduced pressure, not by simple distillation. Statement I is false.

An azeotrope boils at a constant temperature with vapour of the same composition as the liquid, so repeated vaporisation and condensation cannot change the composition and fractional distillation fails to separate it. Statement II is true.

Hence Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

\(S_{N}1\) rates track the stability of the carbocation formed in the rate-determining ionisation step.

Benzyl chloride gives the benzyl cation, whose positive charge is delocalised over the ring by resonance (three extra contributing structures with the charge at ortho and para positions). Ethyl chloride gives the primary ethyl cation, stabilised only by weak hyperconjugation from one methyl group.

So the benzyl cation is far more stable, benzyl chloride ionises faster and reacts faster by \(S_{N}1\). Statement I is true, Statement II is true and it correctly explains Statement I.

The IUPAC seniority order for the principal characteristic group runs carboxylic acid > ester > acid halide > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene/alkyne.

(A) places the ketone \(>C=O\) above \(-CHO\); aldehyde outranks ketone, so (A) is wrong.
(B) places \(-CONH_{2}\) above the ester \(-COOCH_{3}\) (ester is senior to amide) and \(-NH_{2}\) above \(-OH\) (alcohol is senior to amine), so (B) is wrong.
(D) places \(-CHO\) above \(-CN\); nitrile is senior to aldehyde, so (D) is wrong.
(C) gives amide > aldehyde > ketone > amine > alkyne, which follows the seniority list correctly.

The figure shows benzanilide, \(C_{6}H_{5}-CO-NH-C_{6}H_{5}\). Positions r and p lie on the ring bearing the carbonyl group, while s and u lie on the ring bearing the amide nitrogen.

The \(-CO-\) group is electron withdrawing by resonance and induction, so its ring (r, p) is deactivated towards electrophiles. The \(-NH-CO-\) nitrogen still donates its lone pair into its own ring, so that ring is activated and directs ortho/para.

Between the two activated positions, s is ortho to the bulky anilide nitrogen and is sterically blocked, whereas u is the free para position. Electrophilic attack therefore occurs predominantly at u.

(A) Diethylamine (secondary) + ethylamine (primary): the carbylamine test, \(CHCl_{3} + KOH\) with heating, gives a foul-smelling isocyanide only with the primary amine. So (A)-(II).

(B) Acetaldehyde + acetone: ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollens' reagent) gives a silver mirror only with the aldehyde. So (B)-(IV). (The iodoform test would fail here, since both give iodoform.)

(C) Ethanol + phenol: neutral \(FeCl_{3}\) gives a violet colouration only with phenol. So (C)-(III).

(D) Benzoic acid + cinnamic acid: bromine water is decolourised by the \(C=C\) of cinnamic acid but not by benzoic acid. So (D)-(I).

The matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I), which is option (D).

The figures show P = N,N-dimethylaniline, Q = N,N-dimethyl-o-toluidine (one ortho methyl) and R = N,N-dimethyl-2,6-dimethylaniline (two ortho methyls).

Coupling with the benzenediazonium ion is an electrophilic substitution at the position para to nitrogen, and its rate depends on how strongly the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring. That requires the \(NMe_{2}\) group to be coplanar with the ring.

In P there is no ortho substituent, so the group is coplanar and donation is maximum. One ortho methyl in Q twists the bulky \(NMe_{2}\) partly out of plane, and the two flanking methyls in R force it almost perpendicular, so resonance donation is largely lost. This is steric inhibition of resonance.

Hence reactivity follows \(P > Q > R\).

An apple green flame with concentrated HCl is characteristic of \(Ba^{2+}\), which rules out \(Ca^{2+}\) (brick red) and \(Mn^{2+}\) (no characteristic flame).

The group precipitate dissolved in acetic acid and treated with \(K_{2}CrO_{4}\) gives a yellow precipitate of \(BaCrO_{4}\), confirming barium (calcium chromate is soluble, so this test also excludes \(Ca^{2+}\)).

The sodium carbonate extract with concentrated \(HNO_{3}\) and ammonium molybdate gives a canary yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate, \((NH_{4})_{3}PO_{4} \cdot 12MoO_{3}\), which is the confirmatory test for phosphate; sulphate gives no such precipitate.

Hence the salt contains \(Ba^{2+}\) and \(PO_{4}^{3-}\).

\(C_{5}H_{10}\) has one degree of unsaturation. Isomers that do not decolourise \(KMnO_{4}\) contain no \(C=C\), so they are the cycloalkanes: cyclopentane, methylcyclobutane, ethylcyclopropane, 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane and 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane.

Counting distinct types of hydrogen (structural isomers of the monochloro product):

Cyclopentane: all 10 H equivalent, 1 product.
Methylcyclobutane: methyl H, C1 H, C2/C4 H, C3 H, 4 products.
Ethylcyclopropane: ring C1 H, ring C2/C3 H, \(CH_{2}\) of ethyl, \(CH_{3}\) of ethyl, 4 products.
1,1-Dimethylcyclopropane: methyl H and the equivalent ring \(CH_{2}\) H, 2 products.
1,2-Dimethylcyclopropane: methyl H, C1/C2 H, C3 H, 3 products.

Total \(= 1 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 14\).

\(C_{n}H_{2n+2} + \frac{3n+1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow nCO_{2} + (n+1)H_{2}O\).

Given one mole needs 8 mole of oxygen: \(\frac{3n+1}{2} = 8 \Rightarrow 3n + 1 = 16 \Rightarrow n = 5\).
